stemMd:
Infrared imaging recovers the faded entries in the shipyard ledger because the iron in eighteenth-century ink absorbs infrared ______ the paper around it reflects that light back to the camera.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanationMd:
First decide what kind of word group follows the blank. "While the paper around it reflects that light back to the camera" begins with the subordinating conjunction *while*, so it is a dependent clause — it cannot stand on its own.

A dependent clause attached to the end of a main clause takes a comma before the subordinating conjunction when it draws a contrast, and no heavier mark. That gives "...absorbs infrared light, while the paper around it reflects...". Choice C.

Check it with two quick tests. Read the material after the blank on its own: if it is not a sentence, you may not put a period or a semicolon in front of it, which eliminates the two heavy-punctuation choices. Then check that no punctuation separates the conjunction from its own clause, which eliminates choice D.

distractorRationale.b: A period must be followed by a complete sentence. "While the paper around it reflects that light back to the camera" is a dependent clause, so this creates a sentence fragment.
distractorRationale.d: The comma is placed after the subordinating conjunction rather than before it, which cuts "while" off from the clause it introduces. A comma never separates a subordinator from its own clause.
distractorRationale.a: A semicolon joins two independent clauses. The word group after it is dependent, so the semicolon has nothing on its right-hand side that can stand alone as a sentence.

accessibilityText: Choose the option that correctly punctuates the boundary between the words "infrared light" and the clause beginning with the word "while", in a sentence about infrared imaging of a faded ledger.

independentSolve.workingNotes: 'while the paper ... camera' is a subordinate clause of contrast attached to the preceding clause. A comma before a contrastive 'while' is standard, so the answer is (c). (a) puts a semicolon before a dependent clause. (b) makes 'While the paper ... camera.' a fragment. (d) wrongly puts the comma after 'while', separating the conjunction from its own clause.
